title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to create a fake news article impersonating Australian finance presenter Alan Kohler in an interview with Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock. The article falsely claimed discussion of Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, and was part of a broader scam using deepfake content featuring Australian public figures to promote fraudulent investment schemes.

The failure was deployment of generative AI without verification of factual accuracy or identity. The article circulated as a complete news product without human fact-checking or confirmation that the quoted individuals had participated in any such interview. Scammers used the AI-generated content as part of a coordinated deception including fake reviews, advertisements, and investment platforms.

It is not established whether the system was specifically trained to impersonate, or whether it was a general-purpose text generator applied to a malicious use case. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission documented a broader trend of such AI-assisted scams but did not attribute responsibility to any AI provider or system.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article falsely described an interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated story claimed Bullock stormed out over Kohler's questions about the platform. This hoax exemplifies a rising scam trend using artificial intelligence to create deepfake content featuring Australian celebrities and politicians, including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, businesswoman Gina Rinehart, and others, to promote fraudulent investment schemes.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows these scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent. Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Scammers create elaborate deception networks with fake news articles, reviews, and advertisements. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through its public registers before investing and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
